screens.title: Building Your Portfolio & Career in Game Design
screens.narratorSegment: This chapter is about turning your work and practice into a clear, professional signal that studios can evaluate. We’ll show you how to assemble a portfolio that explains your design thinking, write a resume that highlights relevant projects and tools, and choose a career path that matches your strengths. A portfolio is not a gallery of everything you made; it is a curated narrative of three to five strongest projects that reveal how you solve problems and iterate. Your resume should complement that portfolio and speak the language of the role you want. Early-career designers often start generalist and specialize later, so we’ll also cover common design specializations and how to position yourself for them. Finally, you’ll learn practical steps for hosting your portfolio, common pitfalls to avoid, and small habits—like documenting lessons learned—that signal continuous growth. By the end, you’ll know what to show, how to explain it, and how to make a first impression that invites a deeper conversation.

screens.title: Learning Objectives — Growth & Brand
screens.narratorSegment: A sustainable career requires habits that keep your work visible and improving. On this screen we focus on continuous learning and personal branding. Continuous learning means participating in game jams, iterating on small projects, and seeking feedback—practices that produce portfolio-ready artifacts and steady improvement. Personal branding ties your visible work together: a short design philosophy and consistent presentation help recruiters understand who you are as a designer. You will also prepare to document lessons learned for each project so your portfolio entries show reflection and growth. Finally, we emphasize practicing informational interviews and portfolio walkthroughs as ongoing learning tools. These are not one-off tasks; they are part of the long game. Build small habits: update one portfolio project after each major jam, write a 2–3 sentence design philosophy, and curate your top projects quarterly. This steady practice makes your portfolio believable and your brand easier to communicate in an interview.

Module 6 › Chapter 6.5 › Growth & Brand
Continuous Learning & Personal Brand
Small practices that make your portfolio believable and your career sustainable.
Continuous Learning
Participate in game jams, iterate small prototypes, and invite critique regularly. Each cycle should yield a small artifact to add to your portfolio.
Mnemonic: Jam → Iterate → Document
Design Philosophy
Write a 2–3 sentence statement that summarizes your approach and what you value in games.
Example prompt: "I design for emergent player choice through systems that reward experimentation."
Document Lessons
For each project include a short 'lessons learned' note explaining trade-offs and what you'd change next time.
This shows reflection and a growth mindset.
Quarterly Review
Every few months prune weak projects, refresh visuals, and update metrics you can quantify.
Habit: one small update per quarter keeps your portfolio current.

screens.title: Design a Portfolio That Tells a Process
screens.narratorSegment: A game design portfolio is a curated narrative, not an archive. The claim here is simple: employers want to see how you think. That means each chosen project should include a concise overview, artifacts that reveal process, visual evidence of gameplay, and a candid lessons-learned note. For example, if you present a combat system, include a one-paragraph goal statement that explains what you aimed to achieve, a diagram of the combat loop, a short gameplay clip or screenshots, and a short breakdown of your specific contributions. This combination shows intentions, execution, and reflection — the three elements reviewers judge. A common misconception is that more projects equal better odds. In reality, too many weak entries dilute impact. Quality over quantity helps reviewers form a clear mental model of your strengths. Practice curating by selecting three projects that together show breadth and depth: one systems piece, one level or environment, and one UI or narrative example. Final takeaway: choose projects that answer the question, "What design problems did I solve and how did I decide?" Design a Portfolio That Tells a Process means curate 3–5 projects that each state goals, show process artifacts, include visuals, and end with lessons learned.. In practical terms, why curation and process artifacts are more persuasive than volume. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Portfolio rule
keyIdea.text: Curate 3–5 projects that each state goals, show process artifacts, include visuals, and end with lessons learned.

content.html:
Core Concept
Portfolio Structure
Each project entry should make your decisions visible and your impact clear.
  • Overview: What is the project and your role? One short paragraph.
  • Process artifacts: GDD excerpt, flowchart, system diagrams.
  • Visuals: screenshots, short gameplay clips, prototypes.
  • Contributions & lessons: What you did and what you learned.
Key Takeaway

Treat each project as a short case study: goal, process, outcome, lesson.

Concrete Example
Combat System: goal = high-risk, high-reward; include combat loop diagram, ability breakdown, and a 30s gameplay clip to illustrate feel.
Common Mistake
Posting many small unfinished projects without process notes makes it impossible to judge your decision-making.
Project Case Study — Visual Panel
Diagram
Combat Loop: Player Input → Ability Resolve → Enemy Response → Rewards/Costs. Annotate timings and player incentives.
Visuals
Include 2–3 clear screenshots or a single short edited clip showing core mechanics in action.
Process Notes
Explain key trade-offs and a 1–2 sentence lesson learned: what you would change and why.

screens.title: What Each Portfolio Entry Should Include
screens.narratorSegment: Turn a finished or in-progress project into a portfolio entry with a repeatable process. Start with a one-paragraph overview that states the game, your role, and the project's core goal. Next, add process artifacts: excerpts from your game design document, a short flowchart or system diagram, and any wireframes that show decision structure. Then attach visuals: screenshots, concept art, or a short edited gameplay clip—prefer video for clarity when feasible. After that, write a precise contributions list that says what you personally did: mechanics designed, levels authored, scripts implemented, or dialogues written. Finish with a lessons-learned paragraph that explains trade-offs and what you would do differently. A common misconception is to bury your role inside team credits; instead, label your contributions clearly. Use this checklist for every featured project. Practically, you can prepare these pieces in separate files and assemble them into a single web entry or PDF so you can walk through the case study smoothly during a portfolio review. content.html:
Definition
Portfolio Entry Process
Follow this five-step checklist to create consistent case studies.
01
Overview
One paragraph: game, role, and design goal. This sets reviewer expectations immediately.
02
Process Artifacts
Include GDD excerpts, diagrams, or wireframes that reveal your reasoning and iterations.
03
Visuals
Screenshots or a short gameplay video communicate feel faster than text alone.
04
Contributions
List what you specifically designed, implemented, or balanced so the reviewer can judge your work.
05
Lessons Learned
A candid reflection on trade-offs and how you would improve the design shows maturity.
Example: Combat System
Overview: high-risk, high-reward combat system to reward aggressive play. Artifacts: combat loop diagram and ability spreadsheets. Visual: 30s clip of core encounter. Contributions: designed ability cooldowns and balancing. Lesson: reduce burst damage to lower frustration.
Pro Tip
Keep a single slide or page per project for quick walkthroughs. Use timestamps in videos to point to the moment that shows your key decision.

screens.title: Where to Host and How to Present Work
screens.narratorSegment: Choosing where and how to host your portfolio affects discoverability and clarity. The recommended approach is a professional website or a recognized games platform. What matters most is readable structure and high-quality visuals. Use one clear landing page with top projects and direct links to full case studies. Include a short design philosophy and an easy way for recruiters to contact you. Avoid low-quality thumbnails, noisy layouts, or burying your role in team credits. A common mistake is relying on raw videos with no context; always pair videos with a one-paragraph explanation and timestamps. Another mistake is using generic file names or low-resolution screenshots. Host on a personal site or a professional service that preserves image quality and allows simple navigation. For quick sharing in an interview, prepare a PDF or single-page slide that highlights the same material you’ll talk through. The goal is to make it effortless for a reviewer to find your strongest evidence of design thinking. Process Flow
Hosting & Presentation
Preferred hosting: personal site or established game platform. Keep a single landing page and full case studies behind clear links. Always label your role, include a one-paragraph context, and add timestamps for video highlights.

Common Mistake
Low-resolution images or vague role descriptions make it hard to judge you.
Quick Fix
Add a single slide per project and a timestamped video clip for fast walkthroughs.

Case study per project: overview, artifacts, visuals, lessons
Contact info and resume download

screens.title: Design a Resume for Game Roles
screens.narratorSegment: Your resume should be short, scannable, and tailored to the job you seek. Start with a short design philosophy or summary that gives a hiring manager a quick sense of your approach. List relevant projects drawn from your portfolio rather than generic job duties. For each project line, include your role, the tools used, and a quantified outcome if available—metrics like player retention, levels shipped, or jam ranking help when truthful. Use strong action verbs such as designed, balanced, authored, or prototyped. Tailor the top of your resume to match the role: a level-design job should highlight level projects and mapping tools; a technical designer role should emphasize scripting and engine experience. Common errors include long generic resumes or failing to link to your portfolio. Proofread carefully; a single typo can signal carelessness. Finally, keep the layout clean: contact info, summary, selected projects, skills, education or jams, then optional extra links. A well-organized resume guides the reader to your portfolio evidence fast. keyIdea.text: Lead with a short summary, list selected projects with role and tools, and quantify outcomes when possible.

content.html:
Comparison
Resume Structure
Suggested order: Contact → Summary → Selected Projects → Skills → Education/Experience → Links. Keep it to one page for entry-level roles and ensure portfolio links are prominent.
  • Summary: 1–2 sentences of design philosophy
  • Selected Projects: name, your role, tools, and a short measurable outcome
  • Skills: engines, design tools, scripting languages
Key Takeaway

A tailored, proofread resume that points directly to portfolio evidence increases interview chances.

Example Project Line (for resume)
Echoes of the Void — Level & Systems Designer
Tools: Unity, Figma, Spreadsheet balancing
Role: Designed three levels and a procedural map system
Outcome: Improved retention in prototype levels by 15% (playtest)
Use concise bullets and always link the project line to the full case study on your portfolio.

screens.title: Overview of Game Design Career Paths
screens.narratorSegment: The game design field includes several common specializations and understanding them helps you tailor projects and resume entries. Game Designer is a generalist role focused on core gameplay and player experience. Level Designer crafts environments, puzzles, and player paths. Narrative Designer handles story, characters, and dialogue. UI/UX Designer focuses on interfaces and player flow. Technical Designer bridges design and programming with scripting and tools work. Systems Designer focuses on interconnected rules like economy, progression, or combat. Producer manages schedules and team coordination. Many entry-level designers start generalist and specialize as their portfolios and interests mature. To choose a path, review the responsibilities and match them to the projects you enjoy creating. If you like writing branching dialogue, produce a narrative piece. If you enjoy balancing numbers, include a systems project with spreadsheets and explanation. A frequent misconception is that you must pick one forever—specialization often emerges from repeated project choices and the stories you tell in interviews. The practical step is to pick two roles to emphasize in your materials and curate projects that demonstrate those skills. content.html:
Definition
Common Design Specializations
Knowing these roles helps you decide which projects to prioritize.
Game Designer
Core gameplay, mechanics, and player experience.
Level Designer
Environment layout, pacing, and player navigation challenges.
Narrative Designer
Story, characters, and dialogue systems.
UI / UX Designer
Interfaces and user flows that make systems accessible.
Technical Designer
Scripting, tools, and bridging design with engineering.
Systems Designer
Economies, progression, and interlinked gameplay systems.
How to target a role
Select projects that demonstrate the skills required for the role, and use your resume and portfolio summary to state your focus clearly. Start generalist, then specialize through repeated project choices.

screens.title: Building Genuine Industry Connections
screens.narratorSegment: Networking in game design is not about handing out resumes; it’s about building genuine relationships that reveal opportunities over time. Start by treating events and online communities as places to learn and exchange value. At an in-person event, prepare a short, specific conversation opener: mention a talk you enjoyed or a mechanic in a studio’s recent title and ask a question. Online, join targeted Discord servers or LinkedIn groups, comment thoughtfully on discussions, and share useful post-mortems or small design write-ups. A useful habit is to keep a simple contact log: who you met, what you discussed, and one follow-up action. For example, after a game jam, message a teammate with a short note about what you appreciated about their work and offer to share a playable build. Common misconception: networking means asking for a job immediately. Instead, focus on curiosity and reciprocity; offer help, ask for advice, and follow up with concrete, small asks such as an informational chat. Over time these small interactions turn into referrals, invites to collaboration, and mentors who can review your portfolio. Reflect: who in your network could you help this week?

keyIdea.text: Focus on curiosity, follow-up, and small mutual exchanges rather than immediate job requests.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.5 › Building Genuine Connections
Process
A simple 4-step networking rhythm
  1. Prepare: 1–2 talking points about a recent game or talk.
  2. Engage: Ask a question and listen—show curiosity.
  3. Follow-up: Send a 2–3 line message with a resource or thanks.
  4. Nurture: Offer help, ask a short follow-up later.
Quick Tips
  • Keep a contact log with one action per person.
  • Share short lessons from your projects—value attracts replies.
  • Respect time: ask for 15 minutes, not an hour.
Common Mistake

Treating networking as transactional. This leads to shallow connections and fewer long-term opportunities.

Key Takeaway

Small, genuine exchanges build stronger career opportunities than mass outreach.

Scenario
Post-Game Jam Follow-Up
Practical example

Write a 2-line message: thank your teammate, mention one concrete thing you learned, and offer to share the build or a short clip. Attach a single-link to the prototype and one screenshot.

This shows you can communicate concisely and demonstrates your process—more powerful than a long, generic message.

Why it matters

screens.title: Conducting Informational Interviews
screens.narratorSegment: An informational interview is a short, focused conversation where you learn about a role, studio, or career path. The goal is knowledge and relationship-building, not a job pitch. Before the meeting, research the person and their studio—note one specific question about a recent project. Begin by thanking them for their time, briefly stating your background and one learning goal for the chat, then ask open questions: how did they get started, what tools do they use daily, and what skills are most valuable for entry-level designers where they work? During the conversation, practice active listening and take one-page notes. Afterward, send a concise thank-you with a single follow-up item, such as a link to one portfolio excerpt you’d like feedback on. A common misconception is treating it like an interview rehearsal; instead, focus on collecting actionable advice. Example: ask what a level designer at their studio does in the first 90 days—answers clarify realistic expectations and help you tailor your portfolio. Finally, convert the insight into a specific action: update one portfolio entry, practice a skill, or prepare a question for your next meeting. What one change will you make after your next informational interview?

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.5 › Informational Interview
Template: 20-Minute Chat
Agenda
  • Intro (2 min): Quick background & goal.
  • Questions (12 min): Role, daily tasks, skills, studio culture.
  • Wrap (3 min): Ask for one resource or next person to speak to.
Note-taking
Capture one insight and one action. Example: "They use scripted encounters—learn to prototype enemy timing." Action: add a prototype clip to portfolio and note the tools used.
Common Mistake

Asking unfocused or generic questions such as "How do I get a job?" leads to vague answers. Ask targeted questions linked to their role.

Example
Level Designer: First 90 Days

Ask: "What will I be expected to deliver in the first three months?" If they say "blockouts and small puzzles," you can prepare by adding one or two level blockout videos to your portfolio and documenting iteration notes.

Key Takeaway

Use each conversation to create a single, measurable improvement to your portfolio or preparation plan.

screens.title: Preparing for Design Challenges & Portfolio Reviews
screens.narratorSegment: Interview preparation for game design blends practical rehearsal with reflective storytelling. Expect two common segments: a live design challenge and a portfolio walkthrough. For live design prompts, the best approach is to ask clarifying questions, outline constraints, and propose two to three viable solutions with trade-offs. For example, if asked to design a mechanic for a survival horror game emphasizing scarcity, ask about existing economy, intended player pacing, and target platforms. Then propose options: a resource decay system that forces choices, a barter mechanic to trade supplies, or a risk-reward scavenging loop—explain why one fits the stated goals and the trade-offs. For portfolio reviews, prepare concise narratives for each project: goal, your role, a specific design decision, and a measurable outcome or lesson learned. Practice speaking for 2–3 minutes per project, focusing on process rather than polish. A subtle but common mistake is over-justifying decisions with technical detail when the interviewer is looking for design rationale; instead, link choices to player experience. Also rehearse cultural fit stories that demonstrate collaboration and iteration. End prep with a 15-minute mock challenge and a recorded walk-through; reviewing your own explanation sharpens clarity. After interviews, ask one thoughtful question and send a brief thank-you that references a specific point from the conversation. What trade-off will you emphasize in your next mock challenge?

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.5 › Design Challenges
Comparison
Live Challenge vs. Portfolio Review
Live Challenge
Clarify constraints, brainstorm, choose trade-offs.
Portfolio Review
Tell process, highlight your decisions, reflect on lessons.
Common Mistake

Giving a single pitch without exploring trade-offs or failing to show what you learned from iteration.

Walkthrough
3-minute project story
  1. Goal: What player feeling or behavior were you designing for?
  2. Your decision: Which mechanic or change did you choose and why?
  3. Result & lesson: Player reaction, metrics if available, and what you would change next.
Practice Prompt

Design a scarcity mechanic for a horror game. Ask 2 clarifying questions, suggest three options, and pick one with trade-offs. Time yourself and record for review.

screens.title: Continuous Learning and Personal Branding
screens.narratorSegment: Continuous learning is the career engine for game designers. The industry changes quickly, so adopting a growth routine keeps your skills relevant. Make a weekly habit of one focused activity: play and analyze a design you admire, rebuild a small mechanic, participate in a micro jam, or read a post-mortem. Share process work publicly—short write-ups, annotated screenshots, or a five- to ten-second clip of a prototype—to demonstrate thinking. Personal branding is about presenting a consistent design voice across your portfolio, resume, and profiles. A concise design philosophy statement on your portfolio helps recruiters understand your priorities. For example, a statement might emphasize player-centric systems and iterative testing. Avoid treating branding as self-promotion only; instead, share useful insights that reflect your approach. A common misconception is that frequent posting equals branding; quality and focus matter more. Choose two channels you can maintain reliably, such as a portfolio site and one social or community platform, and schedule a small weekly deliverable. Over time, these posts form a public record of progress and attract collaborators and hiring managers. End by picking one micro-skill to practice weekly: what will you commit to for the next month?

screens.title: Portfolio Project Outline & Design Philosophy
screens.narratorSegment: This hands-on activity guides you to prepare a single portfolio entry and a concise design philosophy statement. Choose one project and follow the outline. Start with a clear Project Overview: 1–2 paragraphs describing the game, your role, and the core player experience you targeted. Next, write Design Goals & Challenges: one paragraph listing the objective and the main constraint you faced. For Key Contributions & Process, create a short section for each major contribution. Include a compact visual or short clip and a one-paragraph process note: what you tried, why you chose the solution, and a concrete outcome. In Lessons Learned, reflect on tuning, player feedback, and what you would change next. Finally, add a Playable Demo or video clip if available. For the design philosophy statement, write 2–3 sentences that capture your approach: what you prioritize and why. Example: "I design systems that reward player curiosity through emergent interactions and iterative testing." Avoid generic statements—tie the philosophy to a concrete design habit. After completing the outline, pick one deliverable to finish this week: a 30-second clip, a 300-word design note, or a polished screenshot with captions. Completing this single entry yields a focused, job-ready artifact.

screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.narratorSegment: These three concepts capture the foundation of presenting yourself as a designer. First, a Game Design Portfolio is a curated set of your best work that emphasizes process, choices, and outcomes rather than quantity. Employers use it to see how you think and solve design problems. Second, the Game Design Document or GDD is a living artifact that records vision, mechanics, and systems; including excerpts shows your ability to communicate complex designs. Third, a Resume tailored for games highlights relevant projects, tools, and measurable outcomes; it should use strong verbs and align with the role you seek. Together, these artifacts provide recruiters with evidence of skill, clarity of thought, and professional readiness. When preparing materials, prioritize clarity, honest contribution statements, and one polished example over many incomplete items. Keep these concepts front of mind when networking, interviewing, and iterating on your public presence.

fullNarratorScript:
This chapter is about turning your work and practice into a clear, professional signal that studios can evaluate. We’ll show you how to assemble a portfolio that explains your design thinking, write a resume that highlights relevant projects and tools, and choose a career path that matches your strengths. A portfolio is not a gallery of everything you made; it is a curated narrative of three to five strongest projects that reveal how you solve problems and iterate. Your resume should complement that portfolio and speak the language of the role you want. Early-career designers often start generalist and specialize later, so we’ll also cover common design specializations and how to position yourself for them. Finally, you’ll learn practical steps for hosting your portfolio, common pitfalls to avoid, and small habits—like documenting lessons learned—that signal continuous growth. By the end, you’ll know what to show, how to explain it, and how to make a first impression that invites a deeper conversation.

Over these screens you will gain concrete skills you can use immediately. First, you will learn how to build a compelling game design portfolio that shows your process, not just the finished product. You will practice curating three to five projects and writing concise project entries that reveal your role, goals, and lessons learned. Second, you will master a resume tailored for game design roles: how to highlight tools, measurable impact, and a short design philosophy that communicates your approach. Third, you will identify common career paths within design—level, systems, narrative, UI/UX, technical design—and learn how to target one of them with thoughtful projects. Finally, you will begin to plan networking and interview preparation: where to meet peers, how to present work in a portfolio review, and how to practice design challenges. Each objective is practical: by the end you will have a concrete project outline and a short design philosophy ready to include on a resume or site.

A sustainable career requires habits that keep your work visible and improving. On this screen we focus on continuous learning and personal branding. Continuous learning means participating in game jams, iterating on small projects, and seeking feedback—practices that produce portfolio-ready artifacts and steady improvement. Personal branding ties your visible work together: a short design philosophy and consistent presentation help recruiters understand who you are as a designer. You will also prepare to document lessons learned for each project so your portfolio entries show reflection and growth. Finally, we emphasize practicing informational interviews and portfolio walkthroughs as ongoing learning tools. These are not one-off tasks; they are part of the long game. Build small habits: update one portfolio project after each major jam, write a 2–3 sentence design philosophy, and curate your top projects quarterly. This steady practice makes your portfolio believable and your brand easier to communicate in an interview.

A game design portfolio is a curated narrative, not an archive. The claim here is simple: employers want to see how you think. That means each chosen project should include a concise overview, artifacts that reveal process, visual evidence of gameplay, and a candid lessons-learned note. For example, if you present a combat system, include a one-paragraph goal statement that explains what you aimed to achieve, a diagram of the combat loop, a short gameplay clip or screenshots, and a short breakdown of your specific contributions. This combination shows intentions, execution, and reflection — the three elements reviewers judge. A common misconception is that more projects equal better odds. In reality, too many weak entries dilute impact. Quality over quantity helps reviewers form a clear mental model of your strengths. Practice curating by selecting three projects that together show breadth and depth: one systems piece, one level or environment, and one UI or narrative example. Final takeaway: choose projects that answer the question, "What design problems did I solve and how did I decide?" Design a Portfolio That Tells a Process means curate 3–5 projects that each state goals, show process artifacts, include visuals, and end with lessons learned.. In practical terms, why curation and process artifacts are more persuasive than volume. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Turn a finished or in-progress project into a portfolio entry with a repeatable process. Start with a one-paragraph overview that states the game, your role, and the project's core goal. Next, add process artifacts: excerpts from your game design document, a short flowchart or system diagram, and any wireframes that show decision structure. Then attach visuals: screenshots, concept art, or a short edited gameplay clip—prefer video for clarity when feasible. After that, write a precise contributions list that says what you personally did: mechanics designed, levels authored, scripts implemented, or dialogues written. Finish with a lessons-learned paragraph that explains trade-offs and what you would do differently. A common misconception is to bury your role inside team credits; instead, label your contributions clearly. Use this checklist for every featured project. Practically, you can prepare these pieces in separate files and assemble them into a single web entry or PDF so you can walk through the case study smoothly during a portfolio review. Choosing where and how to host your portfolio affects discoverability and clarity. The recommended approach is a professional website or a recognized games platform. What matters most is readable structure and high-quality visuals. Use one clear landing page with top projects and direct links to full case studies. Include a short design philosophy and an easy way for recruiters to contact you. Avoid low-quality thumbnails, noisy layouts, or burying your role in team credits. A common mistake is relying on raw videos with no context; always pair videos with a one-paragraph explanation and timestamps. Another mistake is using generic file names or low-resolution screenshots. Host on a personal site or a professional service that preserves image quality and allows simple navigation. For quick sharing in an interview, prepare a PDF or single-page slide that highlights the same material you’ll talk through. The goal is to make it effortless for a reviewer to find your strongest evidence of design thinking. Your resume should be short, scannable, and tailored to the job you seek. Start with a short design philosophy or summary that gives a hiring manager a quick sense of your approach. List relevant projects drawn from your portfolio rather than generic job duties. For each project line, include your role, the tools used, and a quantified outcome if available—metrics like player retention, levels shipped, or jam ranking help when truthful. Use strong action verbs such as designed, balanced, authored, or prototyped. Tailor the top of your resume to match the role: a level-design job should highlight level projects and mapping tools; a technical designer role should emphasize scripting and engine experience. Common errors include long generic resumes or failing to link to your portfolio. Proofread carefully; a single typo can signal carelessness. Finally, keep the layout clean: contact info, summary, selected projects, skills, education or jams, then optional extra links. A well-organized resume guides the reader to your portfolio evidence fast. The game design field includes several common specializations and understanding them helps you tailor projects and resume entries. Game Designer is a generalist role focused on core gameplay and player experience. Level Designer crafts environments, puzzles, and player paths. Narrative Designer handles story, characters, and dialogue. UI/UX Designer focuses on interfaces and player flow. Technical Designer bridges design and programming with scripting and tools work. Systems Designer focuses on interconnected rules like economy, progression, or combat. Producer manages schedules and team coordination. Many entry-level designers start generalist and specialize as their portfolios and interests mature. To choose a path, review the responsibilities and match them to the projects you enjoy creating. If you like writing branching dialogue, produce a narrative piece. If you enjoy balancing numbers, include a systems project with spreadsheets and explanation. Choose two channels you can maintain reliably, such as a portfolio site and one social or community platform, and schedule a small weekly deliverable. Over time, these posts form a public record of progress and attract collaborators and hiring managers. End by picking one micro-skill to practice weekly: what will you commit to for the next month?

This hands-on activity guides you to prepare a single portfolio entry and a concise design philosophy statement. Choose one project and follow the outline. Start with a clear Project Overview: 1–2 paragraphs describing the game, your role, and the core player experience you targeted. Next, write Design Goals & Challenges: one paragraph listing the objective and the main constraint you faced. For Key Contributions & Process, create a short section for each major contribution. Include a compact visual or short clip and a one-paragraph process note: what you tried, why you chose the solution, and a concrete outcome. In Lessons Learned, reflect on tuning, player feedback, and what you would change next. Finally, add a Playable Demo or video clip if available. For the design philosophy statement, write 2–3 sentences that capture your approach: what you prioritize and why. Example: "I design systems that reward player curiosity through emergent interactions and iterative testing." Avoid generic statements—tie the philosophy to a concrete design habit. After completing the outline, pick one deliverable to finish this week: a 30-second clip, a 300-word design note, or a polished screenshot with captions. Completing this single entry yields a focused, job-ready artifact.

These three concepts capture the foundation of presenting yourself as a designer. First, a Game Design Portfolio is a curated set of your best work that emphasizes process, choices, and outcomes rather than quantity. Employers use it to see how you think and solve design problems. Second, the Game Design Document or GDD is a living artifact that records vision, mechanics, and systems; including excerpts shows your ability to communicate complex designs. Third, a Resume tailored for games highlights relevant projects, tools, and measurable outcomes; it should use strong verbs and align with the role you seek. Together, these artifacts provide recruiters with evidence of skill, clarity of thought, and professional readiness. When preparing materials, prioritize clarity, honest contribution statements, and one polished example over many incomplete items. Keep these concepts front of mind when networking, interviewing, and iterating on your public presence.

These practical reminders will keep your job search focused. First, Networking is a long-term practice of giving value, following up, and converting brief interactions into ongoing relationships. Second, Design Challenge is an opportunity to show process: clarify constraints, propose multiple solutions, and defend trade-offs tied to player experience. Third, Personal Brand is the public pattern of your work—consistent posts and a short design philosophy make you memorable. Keep these three as active verbs: Connect, Practice, Share. Connect by asking one good question and following up; Practice by rehearsing a design challenge weekly; Share by publishing a small process note tied to a portfolio entry. These steps create momentum that compounds over months, turning practice into opportunities and visibility into offers. What to Remember means turn short actions into enduring career momentum by repeating small, focused habits.. In practical terms, practical reminders to carry into interviews and career development. A simple real-world example is helpful here, because students learn best when they can connect the idea to a familiar situation. This matters because it gives the learner a clear mental model and helps them connect the concept to later examples and problems. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.
